# Piyajātika Sutta (MN 87 (PTS MN ii 106))

**ID:** MN 87 (PTS MN ii 106)  
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)  
**Collection:** Sutta  
**Title (Pali):** Piyajātika Sutta  
**Title (English, from literature):** Born From the Beloved  
**PTS:** MN ii 106  
**tipitaka.org (CST):** [https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0202m.mul3.xml](https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0202m.mul3.xml)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Piyajātika Sutta* ("Born From the Beloved", MN 87; PTS MN ii 106) is the eighty-seventh discourse of the Majjhimanikāya, located in the *Rājavagga* ("Section on Kings") [Galasek 2016]. It is the first of four consecutive suttas in the collection (MN 87–90) featuring King Pasenadi of Kosala [Batchelor 2015]. Set in Jeta's Grove near Sāvatthi, the narrative begins when a grieving householder, devastated by the death of his only son, approaches the Buddha [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. The Buddha informs him that sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are born from and rooted in what is beloved (*piyajātika*) [Galasek 2016; Ngoc Cuong Le 2018]. When the householder and a gathering of gamblers dismiss this teaching, news of the controversy reaches the Kosalan court [Galasek 2016]. King Pasenadi initially rejects the assertion, but Queen Mallikā dispatches the brahman Nāḷijaṅgha to the Buddha to confirm the exact teaching, subsequently guiding the king to insight through a method of cross-questioning regarding his grief should harm befall those he holds dear [Blum 2013; Ngoc Cuong Le 2018].

Curated parallels in Chinese Āgama literature include Madhyama-āgama 216 (MĀ 216), Ekottara-āgama 13.3 (EĀ 13.3), and two individual translations: Taishō 91 (*Boluomen zi mingzhong ainian buli jing*) and Taishō 154.15 [Mei Ching Hsuan 2009].

It also forms part of the traditional Sri Lankan examination curriculum for the *Prācīna Madhyama* grade [ICTS 2017].

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Full parallels: EA 13.3 竹膊; MA 216 愛生; T 154.15 佛說子命過; T 91 婆羅門子命終愛念不離
- Mentioned in: Mnd 15 Attadaṇḍasuttaniddesa

**Sources**

- [Batchelor 2015] Stephen Batchelor, After Buddhism: Rethinking the Dharma for a Secular Age (2015) — Information on the sequence of four consecutive Pasenadi discourses in the Majjhima Nikāya (MN 87–90).
- [Blum 2013] Mark L. Blum (tr.), The Nirvana Sutra (Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra), Vol. I (2013) — Identification of the brahman Nāḷijaṅgha sent by Queen Mallikā to confirm the Buddha's statement.
- [Galasek 2016] Bruno Galasek, On Presenting Characters and Representation of Persons in Narrative Suttas of the Majjhima Nikaya (2016) — Textual location in the Rājavagga, thematic analysis of piyajātika, and mention of the gamblers.
- [ICTS 2017] Proceedings of the International Conference on Tipitaka Studies (2017) — Use of the sutta in the Prācīna Madhyama curriculum in Sri Lanka.
- [Mei Ching Hsuan 2009] Mei Ching Hsuan, Development of Pho ba Liturgy in Medieval Tibet (2009) — Discussion of grief counselling and citation of the Chinese translation T 91.
- [Ngoc Cuong Le 2018] Ngoc Cuong Le, Text and Context: A Hermeneutical Study of the Ways the Buddha Answers Questions (2018) — Queen Mallikā's cross-questioning method with King Pasenadi.
- [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995] Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli and Bhikkhu Bodhi (trs.), The Middle Length Discourses of the Buddha: A Translation of the Majjhima Nikāya (1995) — Setting at Sāvatthi in Jeta's Grove and opening narrative of the householder losing his only son.
